passages.text: Imagine walking into a farm where rows of lettuce, herbs and vegetables are growing neatly in pipes or stacked trays. Their roots are not buried in soil. Instead, they dangle into water, while pumps quietly move a nutrient-rich solution through the system. It may look like farming without one of its most basic ingredients. But hydroponics works by giving plants, in a controlled way, many of the things they normally obtain from soil. So, how does it actually work? What plants get from soil When we think of soil, it is easy to assume that plants “eat” it. In reality, soil mainly acts as a support system and a storehouse from which plant roots access water and essential nutrients. Hydroponics separates these functions. The plant is supported using materials such as coco peat, rockwool, perlite or clay pellets. These materials hold the plant in place but generally do not provide its nutrients. Instead, the nutrients are dissolved in water and delivered directly to the roots. This includes nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, along with calcium, magnesium, sulphur and smaller quantities of elements such as iron and zinc. What Does “Hydroponics” Actually Mean? The direct answer: hydroponics comes from the Greek words for “water” and “labor,” and it describes any growing method where a nutrient solution — water with dissolved minerals — replaces soil as the way a plant gets fed. The word comes from the Greek “hydro,” meaning water, and “ponos,” meaning labor. That definition sounds simple, and mechanically it is. But it’s worth being precise here because “no soil” is doing a lot of work in that sentence. Soil isn’t magic — for a plant, it’s really just performing three jobs: holding the roots in place, storing water, and holding onto dissolved minerals so roots can absorb them. Hydroponics is the growing of plants in a liquid nutrient solution, with or without an artificial medium, using materials like expanded clay, coir, perlite, vermiculite, brick shards, or wood fiber when extra root support is needed (USDA National Agricultural Library).
